idiom_name: Comparable/Comparator with interface default methods; record-synthesised equals/hashCode
implementation_notes: Java has no operator overloading, but the platform standardises exactly the operations it honours: equals/hashCode (every collection and map) and Comparable<T>.compareTo (Collections.sort, TreeMap, Comparator.naturalOrder), with Comparator factories (comparing, thenComparing) supplying derived orderings as default methods. Records generate equals/hashCode from the components, so the value-semantics half costs nothing, and interface default methods are the mixin carrier that lets one interface donate behaviour to a whole family of implementors. Keep Comparable for a single natural ordering and Comparator when several orderings must coexist, and make the natural ordering consistent with equals or sorted collections will violate the Set/Map contracts.
pitfalls: compareTo must be consistent with equals, otherwise TreeSet/TreeMap break the Set/Map contract; the classic trap is a comparison that returns 0 for objects that are not equal.
Generics and primitives do not mix: generic code must take a Comparator/Comparable and pays boxing plus virtual dispatch, so operator-like syntax on value types stays unavailable.
Interface default methods cannot add state, and an inherited implementation wins inside a hierarchy: a subclass cannot quietly opt out of the ordering a superclass already provides.
